cur:catacombs2-zaragoza-receptio-animae.summary: Atlantes support the corners of this crowded frieze, carved in Rome around 330. From left to right Christ heals the woman with an issue of blood, an orant stands between two companions, the soul of the deceased is received by the hand of God (the 'receptio animae' that gives the sarcophagus its name), Christ restores sight to a blind man, and at Cana he touches the water jars with his staff to change water into wine. Its crisp, deeply drilled carving recalls the Roman workshops of the age of Constantine.
facts: Spanish Wikipedia links its workshop stylistically to the sculptors who worked on the Arch of Constantine in Rome.
It comes from the Early Christian necropolis of Zaragoza on this very site and holds relics venerated as those of the 'Santas Masas', the martyrs of Zaragoza.
It was restored in 1998; it is also known as the 'sarcophagus of the Assumption'.

cur:catacombs2-british-museum-gold-glass.summary: From the base of a broken glass bowl, a bust in gold leaf looks out from within two interlaced squares: a youthful figure with curling hair, wearing a tunic and a mantle fastened by a round brooch, with the letters CRIS beside his head. In the corner spaces four small busts surround him. The name identifies the figure as Christ, shown not in a narrative scene but as a portrait at the centre of the vessel.
facts: Gold glasses of this kind, made by sandwiching engraved gold leaf between layers of glass, are mostly known from the catacombs of Rome, where the bases of cups were pressed into the mortar sealing graves.
The number E.C.630 is painted on the fragment, as visible in the photograph.
cur:catacombs2-british-museum-gold-glass.notes: The British Museum catalogue entry was not consulted; date and provenance follow the general type. Only the letters CRIS are clearly legible.

cur:objects-magdeburg-ivory-gerasene-dem.summary: Christ, followed by apostles, raises his hand toward a possessed man, while a small winged demon flees from the man's head and swine rush away at the lower right. The scene is set against a characteristic chequered openwork background, through which a gold ground once shone. It belongs to the series of small plaques that once decorated an altar or pulpit given by Otto I to his new cathedral at Magdeburg.
facts: Wikipedia notes that 16 Magdeburg Ivories survive; they were commissioned by Otto I, probably for the dedication of Magdeburg Cathedral and the raising of the see to an archbishopric in 968, for an object variously conjectured to be an antependium, throne, door or pulpit.
They are often assumed to have been made in Milan, though Peter Lasko argued for artists trained in Lorraine; the openwork backgrounds probably revealed a gilded backing.

cur:objects-pax-of-duke-ursus-cividale.summary: An ivory plaque of the Crucifixion is set in a jewelled silver frame: Christ hangs on the cross, with the Virgin and St John below and busts of the sun and moon in medallions above. Gems of red, green and blue alternate with discs of filigree around the border. Used as a 'pax', it was passed among the faithful to be kissed during Mass, so that the image of the crucified Lord became an instrument of peace.
facts: A pax (or osculatory) was a tablet offered to the clergy and congregation to kiss at the sign of peace during Mass (liturgical use).
It is traditionally associated with a Duke Ursus (Orso) of Friuli, from whom it takes its name; the museum dates it to the mid-9th century.
cur:objects-pax-of-duke-ursus-cividale.notes: The association with Duke Ursus is traditional. Some captions date it 850–900.

cur:objects2-wurzburg-adoration-roundel.summary: Woven in red, yellow, blue and black, this roundel shows the Virgin enthroned frontally with the Christ Child, while the Magi, reduced to bold geometric shapes with large staring eyes, crowd in from the side to offer their gifts. The abstraction of the figures is characteristic of later Coptic tapestry, in which a familiar Gospel scene became almost an emblem.
facts: The museum's label dates the textile to the 7th–8th century and identifies it as wool and linen from Coptic Egypt.
Roundels (orbiculi) like this were sewn onto tunics or furnishing fabrics.

walters:83.730.summary: This narrow Coptic tapestry band, edged with borders of interlace, carries a vertical sequence of schematic figures: at the top a long figure set within a mandorla, then a figure holding a smaller one, and smaller standing figures below. The Walters identifies the scenes, with question marks, as the Virgin and Child, the Baptism and God. Bands of this kind decorated garments and furnishings in early medieval Egypt.
facts: The Walters records it as tapestry-woven, Coptic, and dated 600–900; the material is catalogued only tentatively as wool.
It was given to the Walters in 1978 by Mr. and Mrs. Charles Kilekian of New York.
walters:83.730.notes: The identification of Christ rests on the museum's own tentative title ('Virgin and Child, Baptism, God ?'); the heavily stylised figures cannot be securely read in the photograph. No scripture is given because the subjects are uncertain.
